opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's worth remembering where I was coming from. I had been working in computer vision for decades, and I had seen neural networks come and go. In the late eighties and early nineties there was a lot of excitement, and then it faded because, frankly, on the problems we cared about, the results weren't there. So I was a skeptic, but I'd like to think a principled skeptic. I wasn't against neural networks; I just wanted to see the evidence on the benchmarks that the vision community took seriously.

When Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoff Hinton had their ImageNet result in 2012, that was clearly a big jump on classification. But my reaction, and the reaction of a number of people in the field, was: classification is one thing. Telling you there's a dog somewhere in this image is a relatively coarse task. The problem we had been working on for years was object detection, finding where the objects are and putting boxes around them, and the standard benchmark for that was PASCAL VOC. Methods like deformable part models, which Pedro Felzenszwalb and Ross Girshick and others had developed, had been steadily improving there. So the question in my mind was: does this transfer? Do these features actually help with detection, or is it something specific to the ImageNet classification setup?

So rather than argue about it, we decided to test it. With Ross Girshick, Jeff Donahue and Trevor Darrell, we built what became R-CNN. We took region proposals, ran each one through a convolutional network that had been pretrained on ImageNet, fine-tuned it on the detection data, and evaluated on PASCAL. And the improvement was dramatic, something like a thirty percent relative improvement in mean average precision over the best previous methods, which in a field used to inching forward a point or two a year was enormous.

That was the evidence I needed. It showed two things. First, the representations learned by these networks were genuinely better than the hand-designed features like SIFT and HOG we'd been using. And second, and this was in some ways even more important, they transferred. You could pretrain on a large dataset and then adapt to a different task with less data. Once I saw that, I was convinced, and I think a lot of the vision community converted very quickly after that. Being a scientist means you update when the data tells you to.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you have to remember the context. I had been working in computer vision since the late 1970s, and I had seen neural networks come and go once already. In the 1980s there was the backpropagation era, lots of excitement, and then it fizzled out because the methods didn't scale and the results on real problems weren't convincing. So I was, let's say, a skeptic with a long memory. I was not hostile to the idea, but I wanted evidence.

And for me the evidence had to be on a hard, realistic benchmark where the community had already tried everything else. That's what ImageNet was. By 2012 we had spent a decade building up this machinery, SIFT features, HOG, deformable part models, bag of words with spatial pyramids, and the progress had become incremental. Each year someone would get another percent or two. Then AlexNet came along and cut the error rate almost in half. That's not an incremental improvement. That's a qualitative jump, and it was on a problem that we as a field had defined, with a protocol we trusted, not on some toy dataset that the neural network people had chosen for themselves.

But I'll be honest, even that alone wasn't enough for me, because one result can be a fluke. What really convinced me was what happened in the following year or so. The features learned on ImageNet turned out to transfer. Ross Girshick in my group, with Jeff Donahue and Trevor Darrell, took those features and applied them to object detection on PASCAL VOC, which was the benchmark my community cared about most, and the detection numbers jumped by a huge margin as well. That was R-CNN. So now you had the same basic representation working on classification and on detection, two problems that historically had needed quite different hand-engineered pipelines. At that point the pattern was clear. It wasn't a trick that happened to work on one dataset. It was learning something general about the visual world.

So I would say it took about a year, from late 2012 to late 2013, for me to go from skeptic to convert. And I don't apologize for the skepticism. Science is supposed to work that way. The burden of proof is on the new idea, and in this case the new idea met the burden very decisively.

astra-6.text:
For me, the convincing evidence was performance on a task where we could make a clear comparison. In computer vision, we had spent years developing features and building recognition systems around them. So the question was: could a network learn representations that actually did better than those carefully engineered systems?

The ImageNet results were a very strong signal. But what mattered was that this wasn’t just an isolated result. When these representations proved useful for other vision tasks, such as object detection, the case became much stronger. You could see that the network was learning something broadly useful.

I don’t need a technique to resemble the way I would have designed a solution. I need the experiments to be convincing. If the evidence says it works better, then you have to update your views.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the most convincing evidence was performance on a task where we could make a clear comparison. Image recognition was a good example: you had a fixed dataset, you had a test set, and you could measure how well different approaches worked. If a method produces a substantial improvement under those conditions, you have to take it seriously.

But I would distinguish between being convinced that deep learning works and being convinced that it solves everything. Those are very different claims. You can recognize a powerful new tool and still ask: What is it learning? How well does it generalize? What happens when the conditions change? Those questions remain important.
